lessons.title: What .NET Is: Runtime, SDK, and the CLI
lessons.content:
# What .NET Is: Runtime, SDK, and the CLI

**.NET** is not a language. It is a platform: a runtime that executes your code, a large base class library, and a toolchain. C# is the language most people write on top of it, and this course uses C# throughout.

## The three pieces you install

| Piece | What it is | When you need it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Runtime** | The CLR: JIT compiler, garbage collector, type system | To *run* a .NET app |
| **SDK** | Runtime + compiler + `dotnet` CLI + templates | To *build* a .NET app |
| **BCL** | Base Class Library: `System.*`, collections, IO, networking, JSON | Ships with both |

Installing the SDK gives you everything. Check what you have:

```bash
dotnet --version        # SDK version, e.g. 9.0.100
dotnet --list-runtimes  # every runtime installed side by side
```

## From source to running program

Your C# is compiled to **IL** (Intermediate Language) inside an assembly (`.dll`). The CLR then JIT-compiles that IL into real machine code the first time each method runs. That is why the same `.dll` runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS: the machine-specific step happens at startup, not at build time.

## Your first project

```bash
dotnet new console -o HelloForge   # scaffold a console app
cd HelloForge
dotnet run                         # restore, build, and execute
```

`dotnet new console` writes two files that matter:

```csharp
// Program.cs, top-level statements, no class or Main needed
Console.WriteLine("Hello, .NET!");

var name = Console.ReadLine();
Console.WriteLine($"Welcome to the forge, {name}.");
```

```xml
<!-- HelloForge.csproj, the project file: target framework and dependencies -->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net9.0</TargetFramework>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

`ImplicitUsings` is why `Console` resolves without a `using System;` line, the SDK injects the common namespaces for you.

## The commands you will run daily

```bash
dotnet build            # compile
dotnet run              # build and execute
dotnet test             # run the test projects
dotnet publish -c Release   # produce a deployable folder
dotnet new sln && dotnet sln add MyApp   # group projects in a solution
```

> [!NOTE]
> ".NET Framework" (4.8 and older) is the legacy, Windows-only product. ".NET" with no suffix, versions 5 and up, is the modern cross-platform one, and that is what this course means everywhere. ".NET Core" was the transitional name for versions 1 through 3.1.

lessons.title: Types, Variables, and Control Flow

questions.prompt: What is the type of `total` in `var total = 3 * 1.5;`?
In C#, `string` is a value type copied in full on every assignment.
The `____` operator returns its left operand unless that operand is null, in which case it returns the right one (as in `name ?? "anonymous"`).

lessons.title: Methods, Classes, and Objects

questions.prompt: Which type should you use for currency amounts in C#?
A `record` provides value-based equality without you writing `Equals` yourself.
The `____` keyword on a member means it belongs to the type itself, so you call it without creating an instance.

lessons.title: OOP in .NET: Inheritance, Interfaces, Polymorphism

questions.prompt: How many base classes and interfaces can a single C# class have?
An `abstract` method may include a default body that subclasses can reuse.
A subclass replaces a `virtual` method from its parent using the `____` keyword.

lessons.title: Collections, Generics, and a First Taste of LINQ

questions.prompt: Which collection gives O(1) average lookup by key?
A generic constraint such as `where T : IComparable<T>` is what allows the method body to call `CompareTo` on a `T`.
The LINQ method `____` filters a sequence down to the elements matching a predicate.

lessons.title: Final Project: Console Expense Tracker
lessons.content:
# Final Project: Console Expense Tracker

Build a console application that tracks expenses and persists them to disk. It should exercise every concept from this course: types, classes and records, interfaces, collections, LINQ, exceptions, file IO, and JSON.

## Requirements

1. **Model the domain.** An `Expense` record with `Id` (`Guid`), `Description`, `Amount` (`decimal`), `Category` (an `enum`: Food, Transport, Housing, Fun, Other), and `Date` (`DateOnly`). Keep it immutable and use `with` for edits.
2. **A store behind an interface.** Define `IExpenseStore` with `Add`, `Remove`, `All`, `Save`, and `Load`. Implement it once as `JsonExpenseStore` writing to `expenses.json` through `System.Text.Json`, building the path with `Path.Combine`.
3. **A menu loop.** Read commands with `Console.ReadLine` and dispatch them with a `switch` expression: `add`, `list`, `report`, `delete`, `quit`. Invalid input must never crash the application.
4. **Validation with real exceptions.** Reject a non-positive amount with a custom `InvalidExpenseException`. Parse user input with `decimal.TryParse` and `Enum.TryParse`, not with `try`/`catch` around `Parse`.
5. **A LINQ report.** `report` prints total spend, average expense, spend grouped by category sorted descending, and the three largest expenses. Use `GroupBy`, `Sum`, `OrderByDescending`, and `Take`.
6. **Survive a restart.** Data written in one run must load in the next. Handle a missing or corrupt JSON file by starting empty and telling the user, not by throwing.

## Stretch goals

- Add a `budget <category> <amount>` command, and warn in the report when a category goes over budget.
- Add `export <path>` that writes CSV, and confirm the result opens cleanly in a spreadsheet.
- Add a monthly filter (`report 2026-09`) using `DateOnly` comparisons.
- Split the app into two projects, a class library for the domain plus a console front end, and wire them together with `dotnet add reference`.

Submit a link to your finished repository below. An instructor will review it before you can mark this lesson complete.
